How to read your electricity bill before going solar

Usage rates, supply charges, tariffs and export credits — the five numbers on your bill that decide what solar can actually save you.

Published 17 June 2026Updated 15 October 20267 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

Almost every solar quote you will receive is built from your electricity bill. Yet most people know only one number on it — the total. Reading the bill properly takes ten minutes and changes the quality of every conversation that follows.

The anatomy of a bill

  • Usage charges — the price per kilowatt hour for electricity you consume. On time-of-use tariffs there are several of these, priced differently by time of day.
  • Supply charge — a fixed daily amount covering the connection and metering, paid regardless of how much or how little you use. Solar does not reduce this part.
  • Discounts and adjustments — conditional discounts, concessions, or adjustments that change the amount owed but not the underlying price of energy.
  • Solar or export credits — if you already have solar, what your exports earned, and at what rate per kilowatt hour.
  • Other fees and charges — metering changes, late fees or one-off adjustments.

The three tariff shapes

How the main residential tariff types charge — and how solar interacts with each
Tariff typeHow you are chargedWhat it means for solar
Flat rateOne price per kWh at any time of day, plus supply chargeEvery kilowatt hour of consumption avoided saves the same amount — solar and storage both simply reduce units
Time of useDifferent prices for peak, shoulder and off-peak windowsSolar generates during the shoulder; storage discharges into the expensive peak — timing carries real value
DemandUsage charges plus a capacity charge based on your highest usage over a short interval in a billing periodA single spike can set the charge; battery and load management can shave peaks in ways that solar alone cannot

Which shape you are on — and whether it suits a solar household — is one of the most under-discussed parts of going solar. It is also free to change: the Australian Energy Regulator's Energy Made Easy service compares plans using your actual usage data, and reviewing the plan after solar is installed is often worth more than any hardware upgrade.

The supply charge, and why it never disappears

The daily supply charge covers the cost of being connected: network access, metering and administration. A solar system reduces the usage part of the bill, but the supply charge is paid whether the sun shines or not. A household with a large bill dominated by usage will see dramatic percentage reductions from solar; a household with a modest bill will see a smaller share of the total move. Both outcomes are normal — the arithmetic is just different.

Reading your own bill like an analyst

  1. Find the usage rate — or rates, if you are on time of use. These are the numbers solar will displace.
  2. Find the daily supply charge. This is the floor your bill can never fall below while connected.
  3. Sum the kilowatt hours across four quarters (or one year) — that total is your annual consumption.
  4. Note the export rate if you have solar, and how many kilowatt hours earned it.
  5. Check the seasonality: which quarter is biggest, and is it heating, cooling, or something year-round?

Bill size is a proxy, not a measurement

Two households can pay identical bills while using very different amounts of electricity, because rates differ. When comparing quotes or estimates, always compare kilowatt hours and rates, not dollars alone.

What to bring to a solar enquiry

  • Annual consumption in kWh (summed from bills or downloaded as interval data).
  • Your tariff type and rates, so savings can be valued at the right price.
  • A rough sense of when you use power — mostly daytime, evening, or spread through the day.
  • The supply charge and any export rate, if you already have solar.

Key takeaways

  • The bill's useful numbers are rates, supply charge, annual kWh and export credits — not just the total.
  • Flat, time-of-use and demand tariffs reward solar and storage differently.
  • Supply charges are fixed; solar reduces the usage half of the bill.
  • Interval data turns 'about this much' into an actual hourly profile.
  • Review your plan after installing solar — plan choice multiplies hardware savings.
